section.heading: 8.2 Affine Independence
section.paragraph: This section continues to explore the relation between linear concepts and affine concepts. Consider first a set of three vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , say $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . If $$S$$ is linearly dependent, then one of the vectors is a linear combination of the other two vectors. What happens when one of the vectors is an affine combination of the others? For instance, suppose that
$$\textbf{v}_{3} = \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + t \textbf{v}_{2} , \text{for some} t \text{in} \mathbb{R} .$$
Then
$$\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + t \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{0} .$$
This is a linear dependence relation because not all the weights are zero. But more is true—the weights in the dependence relation sum to $$0$$ :
$$\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) + t + \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) = 0.$$
This is the additional property needed to define affine dependence.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An indexed set of points $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is affinely dependent if there exist real numbers $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ , not all zero, such that
Otherwise, the set is affinely independent.

section.paragraph: An affine combination is a special type of linear combination, and affine dependence is a restricted type of linear dependence. Thus, each affinely dependent set is automatically linearly dependent.

A set $$\{\textbf{v}_{1}\}$$ of only one point (even the zero vector) must be affinely independent because the required properties of the coefficients $$c_{i}$$ cannot be satisfied when there is only one coefficient. For $$\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ , the first equation in (1) is just $$c_{1} = 0$$ , and yet at least one (the only one) coefficient must be nonzero.

Exercise 21 asks you to show that an indexed set $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is affinely dependent if and only if $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{v}_{2}$$ . The following theorem handles the general case and shows how the concept of affine dependence is analogous to that of linear dependence. Parts (c) and (d) give useful methods for determining whether a set is affinely dependent. Recall from Section 8.1 that if $$\textbf{v}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the vector $$\widetilde{\textbf{v}}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ denotes the homogeneous form of $$\textbf{v}$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.paragraph: Given an indexed set $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , with $$p \geq 2$$ , the following statements are logically equivalent. That is, either they are all true statements or they are all false.

list.item: One of the points in $$S$$ is an affine combination of the other points in $$S$$ .﻿
The set $$\{\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent.
The set $$\{{\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{1},\ldots,{\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{p}\}$$ of homogeneous forms in $$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ is linearly dependent.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose statement (a) is true, and let $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ satisfy (1). By renaming the points if necessary, one may assume that $$c_{1} \neq 0$$ and divide both equations in (1) by $$c_{1}$$ , so that $$1 + (c_{2}/c_{1}) + \cdots + (c_{p}/c_{1}) = 0$$ and
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left(\right. - c_{2} / c_{1} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + \left(\right. - c_{p} / c_{1} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{p}$$

Note that the coefficients on the right side of (2) sum to 1. Thus (a) implies (b). Now, suppose that (b) is true. By renaming the points if necessary, one may assume that $$\textbf{v}_{1} = c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$$ , where $$c_{2} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ . Then
$$\left(\right. c_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} = c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \textbf{v}_{p}$$
and
$$c_{2} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + \hdots + c_{p} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) = \textbf{0}$$
Not all of $$c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}$$ can be zero because they sum to $$1$$ . So (b) implies (c).

Next, if (c) is true, then there exist weights $$c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}$$ , not all zero, such that (4) holds. Rewrite (4) as (3) and set $$c_{1} = - (c_{2} + \cdots + c_{p})$$ . Then $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 0$$ . Thus, (3) shows that (1) is true. So (c) implies (a), which proves that (a), (b), and (c) are logically equivalent. Finally, (d) is equivalent to (a) because the two equations in (1) are equivalent to the following equation involving the homogeneous forms of the points in $$S$$ :
$$c_{1} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{1} 1 \left]\right. + \hdots + c_{p} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{p} 1 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 0 0 \left]\right.$$

In statement (c) of Theorem 5, $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ could be replaced by any of the other points in the list $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ . Only the notation in the proof would change. So, to test whether a set is affinely dependent, subtract one point in the set from the other points, and check whether the translated set of $$p - 1$$ points is linearly dependent.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The affine hull of two distinct points $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ is a line. If a third point $$\textbf{r}$$ is on the line, then $$\{\textbf{p},\textbf{q},\textbf{r}\}$$ is an affinely dependent set. If a point $$\textbf{s}$$ is not on the line through $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ , then these three points are not collinear and $$\{\textbf{p},\textbf{q},\textbf{s}\}$$ is an affinely independent set. See Figure 1.

image.alt: A figure shows a slanted line labeled aff OpenCurlyBracket p, q close brace passing through the points r, p, and q. A point s is seen below the line near the point q.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . Determine whether $$S$$ is affinely independent.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Compute $$\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ {- .5} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ These two points are not multiples and hence form a linearly independent set, $$S\prime$$ . So all statements in Theorem 5 are false, and $$S$$ is affinely independent. Figure 2 shows $$S$$ and the translated set $$S\prime$$ . Notice that $$\text{Span} S\prime$$ is a plane through the origin and $$\text{aff} S$$ is a parallel plane through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . (Only a portion of each plane is shown here, of course.)

image.alt: A three dimensional graph shows a tilted rectangular plane along with its affinely independent set, depicted by another parallel plane placed over it.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 14 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and let $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ . Is $$S$$ affinely dependent?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Compute $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ - .5 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 11 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and row reduce the matrix:

$$\left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 4 & 1 & 11 - .5 & 0 & - 1 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 0 & 5 & 15 0 & - .5 & - 1.5 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 0 & 5 & 15 0 & 0 & 0 \left]\right.$$

Recall from Section 4.5 (or Section 2.8) that the columns are linearly dependent because not every column is a pivot column; so $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ are linearly dependent. By statement (c) in Theorem 5, $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3},\textbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is affinely dependent. This dependence can also be established using (d) in Theorem 5 instead of (c).

section.paragraph: The calculations in Example 3 show that $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , which means that $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ . By Theorem 1 in Section 8.1, $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ is in $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . In fact, complete row reduction of the matrix in Example 3 would show that
$$\mathbf{v}_{4} - \mathbf{v}_{1} & = & 2 \left(\right. \mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + 3 \left(\right. \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} \left.\right)$$
$$\mathbf{v}_{4} & = & - 4 \mathbf{v}_{1} + 2 \mathbf{v}_{2} + 3 \mathbf{v}_{3}$$
See Figure 3.

image.alt: A three dimensional graph shows an affinely independent set of four vectors given by a tilted rectangular plane on top of another similar plane.

figure.caption: Figure 3 v4 is in the plane ﻿ aff {v1,v2,v3}

section.paragraph: Figure 3 shows grids on both $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}\}$$ and $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . The grid on $$\text{aff} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}\}$$ is based on (5). Another “coordinate system” can be based on (6), in which the coefficients $$- 4 ,$$ $$2$$ , and $$3$$ are called affine or barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ .﻿
section.heading: Barycentric Coordinates
section.paragraph: The definition of barycentric coordinates depends on the following affine version of the Unique Representation Theorem in Section 4.4. See Exercise 25 in this section for the proof.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿6﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿6﻿
note.paragraph: Let $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ be an affinely independent set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Then each $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{aff} S$$ has a unique representation as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ . That is, for each $$\textbf{p}$$ there exists a unique set of scalars $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$$ such that

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ be an affinely independent set. Then for each point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{aff} S$$ , the coefficients $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$$ in the unique representation (7) of $$\textbf{p}$$ are called the barycentric coordinates (or, sometimes, affine) of $$\textbf{p}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Observe that (7) is equivalent to the single equation
$$\left[\right. p 1 \left]\right. = c_{1} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{1} 1 \left]\right. + \hdots + c_{k} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{k} 1 \left]\right.$$

involving the homogeneous forms of the points. Row reduction of the augmented matrix $$\lbrack\begin{matrix} {\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{1} & \cdots & {\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{k} & \widetilde{\textbf{p}} \end{matrix}\rbrack$$ for (8) produces the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Find the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ determined by the affinely independent set $$\left\{ \textbf{a},\textbf{b},\textbf{c} \right\}$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Row reduce the augmented matrix of points in homogeneous form, moving the last row of ones to the top to simplify the arithmetic:

$$\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\overset{\sim}{\mathbf{a}} & \overset{\sim}{\mathbf{b}} & \overset{\sim}{\mathbf{c}} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 3 & 9 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 & 3 & 3\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix} \\ ∼ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{5}{12}\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix}$$
The coordinates are $$\frac{1}{4}$$ , $$\frac{1}{3}$$ , and $$\frac{5}{12}$$ , so $$\textbf{p} = \frac{1}{4}\textbf{a} + \frac{1}{3}\textbf{b} + \frac{5}{12}\textbf{c}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Barycentric coordinates have both physical and geometric interpretations. They were originally defined by A. F. Moebius in 1827 for a point $$\textbf{p}$$ inside a triangular region with vertices $$\textbf{a}$$ , $$\textbf{b}$$ , and $$\textbf{c}.$$ He wrote that the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ are three nonnegative numbers $$m_{\textbf{a}}$$ , $$m_{\textbf{b}}$$ , and $$m_{\textbf{c}}$$ such that $$\textbf{p}$$ is the center of mass of a system consisting of the triangle (with no mass) and masses $$m_{\textbf{a}}$$ , $$m_{\textbf{b}}$$ , and $$m_{\textbf{c}}$$ at the corresponding vertices. The masses are uniquely determined by requiring that their sum be $$1$$ . This view is still useful in physics today.1

Figure 4 gives a geometric interpretation to the barycentric coordinates in Example 4, showing the triangle $$\Delta\textbf{abc}$$ and three small triangles $$\Delta\textbf{pbc}$$ , $$\Delta\textbf{apc}$$ , and $$\Delta\textbf{abp}$$ . The areas of the small triangles are proportional to the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ . In fact,

$$\text{area} \left(\right. \Delta \textbf{pbc} \left.\right) & = & \frac{1}{4} \cdot \text{area} ( \Delta \textbf{abc} ) \text{area} \left(\right. \Delta \textbf{apc} \left.\right) & = & \frac{1}{3} \cdot \text{area} ( \Delta \textbf{abc} ) \text{area} \left(\right. \Delta \textbf{abp} \left.\right) & = & \frac{5}{12} \cdot \text{area} ( \Delta \textbf{abc} )$$

image.alt: A figure shows a tilted tetrahedron with an area of three faces.

figure.caption: Figure 4 p=ra+sb+tc. Here,﻿ r=14, ﻿ s=13, ﻿ t=512

section.paragraph: The formulas in Figure 4 are verified in Exercises 29–31. Analogous equalities for volumes of tetrahedrons hold for the case when $$\textbf{p}$$ is a point inside a tetrahedron in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , with vertices $$\textbf{a}$$ , $$\textbf{b}$$ , $$\textbf{c},$$ and $$\textbf{d}$$ .﻿

When a point is not inside the triangle (or tetrahedron), some of the barycentric coordinates will be negative. The case of a triangle is illustrated in Figure 5, for vertices $$\textbf{a}$$ , $$\textbf{b}$$ , $$\textbf{c}$$ , and coordinate values $$r$$ , $$s$$ , $$t$$ , as above. The points on the line through $$\textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{c}$$ , for instance, have $$r = 0$$ because they are affine combinations of only $$\textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{c}.$$ The parallel line through $$\textbf{a}$$ identifies points with $$r = 1$$ .﻿

section.heading: Barycentric Coordinates in Computer Graphics
section.paragraph: When working with geometric objects in a computer graphics program, a designer may use a “wire-frame” approximation to an object at certain key points in the process of creating a realistic final image. For instance, if the surface of part of an object consists of small flat triangular surfaces, then a graphics program can easily add color, lighting, and shading to each small surface when that information is known only at the vertices. Barycentric coordinates provide the tool for smoothly interpolating the vertex information over the interior of a triangle. The interpolation at a point is simply the linear combination of the vertex values using the barycentric coordinates as weights.

Colors on a computer screen are often described by RGB coordinates. A triple $$(r,g,b)$$ indicates the amount of each color—red, green, and blue—with the parameters varying from $$0$$ to $$1.$$ For example, pure red is $$(1,0,0)$$ , white is $$(1,1,1)$$ , and black is $$(0,0,0)$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 3.5 \end{bmatrix}.$$ The colors at the vertices $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ of a triangle are magenta $$(1,0,1)$$ , light magenta $$(1,.4,1)$$ , and purple $$(.6,0,1)$$ , respectively. Find the interpolated color at $$\textbf{p}$$ . See Figure 6.

image.alt: A figure shows a triangle with interpolated colors.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, find the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ . Here is the calculation using homogeneous forms of the points, with the first step moving row $$4$$ to row $$1$$ :

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\overset{\sim}{v}_{1} & \overset{\sim}{v}_{2} & \overset{\sim}{v}_{3} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 & 3 \\ 5 & 4 & 1 & 3.5\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & .25 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & .50 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & .25 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

So $$\textbf{p} = .25\textbf{v}_{1} + .5\textbf{v}_{2} + .25\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Use the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ to make a linear combination of the color data. The RGB values for $$\textbf{p}$$ are
$$.25 \left[\right. 1 0 1 \left]\right. + .50 \left[\right. 1 .4 1 \left]\right. + .25 \left[\right. .6 0 1 \left]\right. = \left[\right. .9 .2 1 \left]\right. \text{red} \text{green} \text{blue}$$

section.paragraph: One of the last steps in preparing a graphics scene for display on a computer screen is to remove “hidden surfaces” that should not be visible on the screen. Imagine the viewing screen as consisting of, say, a million pixels, and consider a ray or “line of sight” from the viewer’s eye through a pixel and into the collection of objects that make up the $$3D$$ display. The color and other information displayed in the pixel on the screen should come from the object that the ray first intersects. See Figure 7. When the objects in the graphics scene are approximated by wire frames with triangular patches, the hidden surface problem can be solved using barycentric coordinates.

image.alt: A figure shows a grid plane in between an eye and a group of solid objects kept at varying distances.

figure.caption: Figure 7 A ray from the eye through the screen to the nearest object

section.paragraph: The mathematics for finding the ray-triangle intersections can also be used to perform extremely realistic shading of objects. Currently, this ray-tracing method is too slow for real-time rendering, but recent advances in hardware implementation may change that in the future.2

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let

$$v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 11 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & a = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & b = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.7 \\ .4 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$

and $$\textbf{x}(t) = \textbf{a} + t\textbf{b}$$ for $$t \geq 0$$ . Find the point where the ray $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ intersects the plane that contains the triangle with vertices $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Is this point inside the triangle?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The plane is $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . A typical point in this plane may be written as $$(1 - c_{2} - c_{3})\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3}\textbf{v}_{3}$$ for some $$c_{2}$$ and $$c_{3}$$ . (The weights in this combination sum to $$1$$ .) The ray $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ intersects the plane when $$c_{2}$$ , $$c_{3}$$ , and $$t$$ satisfy
$$\left(\right. 1 - c_{2} - c_{3} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{a} + t \textbf{b}$$

Rearrange this as $$c_{2}\left( \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) + c_{3}\left( \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) + t\left( - \textbf{b} \right) = \textbf{a} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ . In matrix form,

$$[ \begin{matrix}\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} & \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} & - \mathbf{b}\end{matrix} ] & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}c_{2} \\ c_{3} \\ t\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{v}_{1}$$
For the specific points given here,

$$v_{2} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & v_{3} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 10 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & a - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 1 \\ 16\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Row reduction of the augmented matrix above produces

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 & 4 & - .7 & - 1 \\ 0 & 10 & - .4 & - 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 16\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & .3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & .1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Thus $$c_{2} = .3$$ , $$c_{3} = .1$$ , and $$t = 5$$ . Therefore, the intersection point is
$$x \left(\right. 5 \left.\right) = a + 5 b = \left[\right. 0 0 10 \left]\right. + 5 \left[\right. .7 .4 - 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 3.5 2.0 - 5.0 \left]\right.$$
Also,

$$\mathbf{x} \left(\right. 5 \left.\right) & = & \left(\right. 1 - .3 - .1 \left.\right) \mathbf{v}_{1} + .3 \mathbf{v}_{2} + .1 \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & .6 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. + .3 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. + .1 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 11 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3.5 \\ 2.0 \\ - 5.0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
The intersection point is inside the triangle because the barycentric weights for $$\textbf{x}(5)$$ are all positive.

list.item: Describe a fast way to determine when three points are collinear.

The points $$v_{1} = \left[\right. 4 1 \left]\right. ,$$ $$v_{2} = \left[\right. 1 0 \left]\right. ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ form an affinely dependent set. Find weights $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{4}$$ that produce an affine dependence relation ﻿ $$c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{4}\textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{0}$$ , where $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{4} = 0$$ and not all $$c_{i}$$ are zero. [Hint: See the end of the proof of Theorem 5.]
